Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 100, verse 1:

Page 60
(Surat al-'Adiyat)
Eleven verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By the chargers, panting﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the chargers, panting﴾.

Know that ad-dabh (the panting) is the sound of the breaths of horses when they run. It is a sound that is neither neighing (sahil) nor whinnying (hamhama), but the sound of breathing. Then they differed about what is meant by al-'adiyat (the chargers) into two opinions:

The first: what is related from 'Ali, peace be upon him, and Ibn Mas'ud, that they are the camels. This is also the view of Ibrahim and al-Qurazi. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While I was sitting in al-Hijr, a man came to me and asked me about al-'adiyati dabhan (the chargers, panting), and I explained them as horses. He went to 'Ali, peace be upon him, who was beneath the water-supply of Zamzam, asked him, and mentioned to him what I had said. He said: 'Bring him to me.' When I stood over him, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of. By Allah, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad. ﴿By the chargers, panting﴾ refers to camels from 'Arafa to Muzdalifa, and from Muzdalifa to Mina, meaning the camels of the pilgrims.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: "So I returned from my view to the view of 'Ali, peace be upon him."

This view is reinforced by what Ubayy related concerning the merit of the surah, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever recites it will be given a reward equal to the number of those who spent the night at Muzdalifa and witnessed the gathering (jam')."

On this view, ﴿Then those who strike sparks, striking﴾ means that the hooves strike the stones from the intensity of the running, so they strike another stone and kindle fire. Or the meaning is: those who ride the camels, who are the pilgrims, when they kindle their fires at Muzdalifa. ﴿Then those who make a raid at dawn﴾: al-ighara is swiftness of travel, and they rush at the morning of the day of sacrifice, hastening towards Mina. ﴿Then raise thereby dust﴾ means raising dust by running. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "The naq' (dust) is what lies between Muzdalifa and Mina." ﴿Then penetrate thereby into the midst of the gathering﴾ means Muzdalifa, because it is called the Jam' (gathering) on account of the gathering of the pilgrims there. On this interpretation, the ways in which Allah swears by it are several:

The first: what we have mentioned of the abundant benefits in it, in His saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camels?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17].

The second: it is as if it is an allusion to the ungrateful human being (al-kanud). It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "I have subjected the like of this to you, and yet you rebel against My obedience."

The third: the purpose of mentioning the camels of the pilgrimage is to encourage Hajj. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "I have made those camels a subject of oath, so how would I waste your deed?" And in it is an allusion to whoever desires Hajj, for al-kanud is the ungrateful one, and whoever does not perform Hajj after it has become obligatory is described by that, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage to the House … and whoever disbelieves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97].

The second opinion: the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, 'Ata' and most of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun): that it refers to horses. This is also related as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Al-Kalbi said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a detachment (sariyya) to some people from Kinana. He remained as long as Allah willed him to remain, and no news came to him from them, so he feared for it. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with news of its march."

If we take the alif and lam in ﴿al-'adiyat﴾ to refer to a previously known thing (al-ma'hud al-sabiq), then the object of the oath is the horses of that detachment. If we take them to indicate the genus (lil-jins), then it is an oath by every horse that runs in the way of Allah.

Know that the wording of these verses indicates that the intended meaning is horses, because dabh occurs only for the horse, and the use of this word for camels is by way of metaphor (isti'arah), just as the lips (mashafir) and hoof (hafir) are used for a human being, and the two lips (shafatan) for a foal. Departing from the literal meaning to the metaphorical without necessity is not permissible. Also, striking sparks is more evident with the hoof than with the sole of the camel, and likewise His saying: ﴿Then those who make a raid at dawn﴾, because that is easier with horses than with other animals. We have related that it came in some of the detachments. If this is so, then the closer view is that the surah is Madani, because permission to fight was given in Medina. This is what al-Kalbi said.

Having understood that, there are here several issues:

The first issue: Allah, exalted is He, swore only by horses because they have praiseworthy qualities in running that other beasts do not have. They are suitable for pursuit and for flight, for attack and for retreat. When you think that benefit lies in pursuit, you run toward the enemy to win the spoils; and when you think that the interest lies in flight, you are able to run at the greatest speed. There is no doubt that safety is one of the two gains. So Allah, exalted is He, swore by the mount of the warrior because of what it contains of the benefits of this world and the religion. In this is an alert that a person must keep it not for adornment and boasting, but for this benefit. Allah, exalted is He, has already drawn attention to this meaning in His saying: ﴿And the horses and mules and donkeys, that you may ride them and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. He placed the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) before riding and did not place it before adornment. As for His saying ﴿panting﴾, it is because it is a sign by which it shows fatigue, and that it expends its full effort and does not stop at exhaustion. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "Despite its weakness, it does not abandon your obedience; so let the servant too be like this in obedience to his Master."

The second issue: They have mentioned several views concerning the parsing (i'rab) of ﴿dabhan﴾:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: "al-'adiyat tadbahu dabhan" (the chargers pant, panting).

The second: that ﴿al-'adiyat﴾ carries the meaning of al-dabihat (those that pant), because dabh occurs with running. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The third: the Basrans said: the estimate is "al-'adiyat dabihatan" (running, panting), so His saying ﴿dabhan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 100, verse 2:

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By those that strike sparks, striking﴾.

Know that al-iraa' (إيراء, the producing of fire) is bringing out fire, and al-qad'h (القدح, striking) is percussion. You say: "qadaha fa-awra" (he struck and so produced fire) and "qadda fa-asla'" (he struck and so produced fire from flint). Then, concerning the interpretation of the verse, there are several views:

Page 62

The first: Ibn Abbas said: it means the horses striking the mountain with their hooves, so that fire is produced from it like the tinder when it is struck. Muqatil said: it refers to the horses that strike sparks with their hooves on the stones, fire like the fire of al-Hubahib. Al-Hubahib is the name of a man who was stingy and would kindle a fire only when people were asleep; when anyone woke, he would put out his fire so that no one would benefit from it. So this fire that springs from the horses' hooves is likened to that fire from which there was no benefit. Some people say it is the iron of the horseshoe striking the rock so that fire comes out; but the first is more eloquent, because on that interpretation the hooves themselves would be like iron.

The second: a group said: these verses are about horses, but their producing fire means that they stir up war between their riders and their enemy, as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. From this comes the saying of war, when it engages: "hami al-watis" (the oven has become hot).

The third: they are the people who raid and at night kindle their fires for their needs and their food. ﴿By those that strike sparks﴾ means the groups of raiders.

The fourth: it is the tongues, which kindle the fire of enmity because of the greatness of what they say.

The fifth: it is the thoughts of men, which kindle the fire of scheming and deception; this is narrated from Ibn Abbas. It is said: "La-aqdahanna laka thumma la-uwariyanna laka," meaning: I will surely stir up evil and war against you. It was also said: it is trickery, except that it is trickery by kindling fire so that the enemy sees them as many. It is a custom of the Arabs, when raiding and approaching the enemy, to kindle many fires so that when the enemy looks at them, he thinks them numerous.

The sixth: Ikrimah said: "al-muriyat qadhan" (those that strike sparks) are the spear-points.

The seventh: ﴿By those that strike sparks﴾, that is, by those who achieve their aims, meaning those who have found what they sought and attained their objective in the raid and the pilgrimage. It is said of one who succeeds in his need: "warra zanduhu" (his firestriker produced fire). This returns to the successful group, and it is also possible that it refers to the horses, whose riders succeed. Jarir said:

We found the Azd most generous in giving, and most productive of fire when they strike the tinder.

It is also said: "So-and-so, when he strikes, produces fire, and when he gives, makes others flow" (or "gives abundantly"). Know that the first view is closer, because the word al-iraa' is literally used for producing fire, and its use in other senses is metaphorical, and it is not permissible to abandon the literal meaning without evidence.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 100, verses 3–4:

As for His saying, ﴿By the raiders at dawn﴾, it means the horses that raid the enemy at the time of dawn. The Arabs used to raid in the morning because at night they would be in darkness and could not see anything, whereas in the daytime people are prepared for defence and fighting. At this time, however, people are in heedlessness and unpreparedness. As for those who interpreted these verses as referring to camels, they said: the meaning is the camels that push on with their riders on the Day of Sacrifice from Jam' to Mina, and the sunnah is not to hasten (ughayyir) until it is morning. The meaning of al-ighara (raiding) in the language is hastening; it is said: aghara if he hastened. The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to say: "Ashriq Thabir, kay nughir" (Shine forth, Thabir, so that we may hasten), that is, "so that we may hasten in the departure."

As for His saying, ﴿and then raise up dust therewith﴾, there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: regarding al-naq' (dust) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is the dust. It was said: it is derived from naq' al-sawt (the raising of a voice) when it rises, so dust is called naq' because of its rising. It was also said: it is from al-naq' in water, as if the one who raises the dust has plunged into it, just as a man plunges into water.

The second: al-naq' is the outcry, from his saying, peace be upon him: "There was no naq' and no laqlaqa" (no wailing and no clamour), that is, they stirred up in the enemy's place the cries of mourners, and their voices rose. It is said: "thara al-ghubar wa al-dukhan," meaning it rose and was stirred up; and "tha'ara al-qata 'an mifhasihi" (the sand-grouse rose from its nest); and "atharna al-ghubar," meaning they stirred it up. The meaning is that the horses raised dust because of the intensity of the running at the place where they made the raid.

The second issue: to what does the pronoun in His saying "bihi" (therewith) refer? There are several possibilities:

The first of them, and this is the statement of al-Farra', is that it refers to the place which they reached, the location where the raid takes place, because in His saying ﴿By the raiders at dawn﴾ there is an indication that the raid must have a place. When the meaning is known, it is permissible to allude to what it is not permissible to mention explicitly, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

The second: it refers to that time in which the raid took place, meaning: they raised dust at that time.

The third, and this is the statement of al-Kisa'i, is that it refers to the running (al-'adw), meaning: they raised dust by the running, and the mention of the running has already passed in His saying: ﴿By the racers﴾.

The third issue: If it is asked, upon what is His saying ﴿and raise up﴾ conjoined? We say: upon the verb which the active participle has been put in place of, and the estimate is: "those who ran and then struck sparks, and raided and then raised dust."

The fourth issue: Abu Haywa read "fa-atharna" with the doubling (shadda), meaning "then they made dust appear therewith," because ta'thir (making an impression/stirring) carries the sense of making appear; or it is a transposition of "thawwarna" into "watthurna," and the waw was changed to a hamza.

The commentary of al-Razi on surah 100, verse 5:

As for His saying, ﴿and thereby penetrate into the midst of a gathering﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: Al-Layth said: "I penetrated (wasatu) the river and the desert, I penetrate it (ausutuha) with wasaṭan and wisaṭatan, meaning I came to be in its middle (wasaṭ). Likewise, I made it penetrated (wassaṭtuha) and I penetrated it (tawassaṭtuha), and similar to this." Al-Farra' said: "The pronoun in His saying ﴿thereby﴾, to what does it refer?" There are several views on this.

The first: Muqatil said: it refers to the charge (al-'adw). That is because the chargers (al-'adiyat) indicate the charge, so the reference was made to it indirectly. His saying ﴿a gathering﴾ means a gathering of the enemy. The meaning is: they then came to be in the midst of a gathering of the enemy. As for whoever takes the verses to refer to camels, he says: it means the gathering at Mina.

The second: the pronoun refers to the dust (al-naq'), meaning: ﴿they penetrate﴾ with the dust the gathering.

The third: the meaning is that the chargers penetrated, clothed in dust, a gathering from the gatherings of the enemies.

The second issue: It was read as ﴿fa-wassatna﴾ with the shadda (gemination) for transitivity, and the particle "bi" (with) is extra, for emphasis, like His saying ﴿so bring him﴾ [al-Anbiya: 61]. It is an intensification of "wassatna". Know that people have said a great deal about the description of the horse, and this amount which Allah mentioned is the best. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Goodness is tied to the forelocks of horses," and he (ﷺ) also said: "Their backs are a protection and their bellies are a treasure." Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the thing sworn by, He mentioned the thing sworn about, which consists of three matters:

The first matter is His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The root of kanud (ungrateful) is withholding what is right and good, and the kanud is one who withholds what is owed. And a kanud land is one that produces nothing. Then the exegetes have various expressions. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: the kanud is the kafur (ungrateful disbeliever). They said: from it the famous man was named Kindah, because he disowned (kanada) his father and separated from him. And from al-Kalbi: the kanud, in the language of Kindah, is the disobedient one; in the language of Banu Malik, the stingy one; and in the language of Mudar and Rabi'ah, the ungrateful one. Abu Umamah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "the kanud is the ungrateful one who withholds his gift, eats alone, and beats his servant." Al-Hasan said: "al-kanud" is one who complains to his Lord, counting trials and calamities, and forgets blessings and comforts. This is like His saying: ﴿But as for man, when his Lord tries him and honours him and bestows favour upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tries him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ [al-Fajr: 16]. Know that the meaning of kanud does not go beyond being disbelief or wickedness, and in any case it cannot be applied to all people, so it must be restricted to a particular disbeliever. Or, if we apply it to all, the meaning is that human nature inclines him to this, except when Allah protects him from it by His kindness and grace. The first view is that of the majority. They said: because Ibn Abbas said that it was revealed concerning Qurt ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Nawfal al-Qurashi. Also, His saying: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾ befits only the disbeliever, since it is like an indication that he denies that matter.

The second: among the matters over which Allah swore is His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾, and concerning it there are two views:

One: that man, to that (i.e., to his ingratitude), is a witness, testifying against himself to it, either because it is a clear matter that he cannot deny, or because he will testify against himself to it in the Hereafter and acknowledge his sins.

The second view: the intended meaning is "And indeed Allah is, to that, a witness." They said: this is preferable, because the pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned item, and the nearest here is the word "Lord" (Rabb), exalted is He. This would be like a warning and a deterrent to him from disobedience, in that He records his deeds against him. As for those who support the first view, they said: since His following saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾ has its pronoun referring to man, it is necessary that the pronoun in the verse before it also refer to man, so that the arrangement is better.

The third matter over which Allah swore is His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾. Khayr (good) here means wealth, from His saying: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth (khayran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180] and His saying: ﴿And when evil (sharr) touches him, he is despairing﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 21]. This is because people count wealth among themselves as good, just as He, exalted is He, called what the fighter receives of wounds and the harm of war "evil (su')" in His saying: ﴿no harm (su') touched them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 174]. Al-shadid means the stingy, withholding one; it is said: "so-and-so is shadid and mutashaddid." Tarafah said:

I see death seizing the noble and choosing the treasured wealth of the wicked, miserly one.

Then in the interpretation there are several aspects:

One: that because of love of wealth, he is indeed stingy and withholding.

Second: that the intended meaning of shadid is strong, and the meaning is: "And indeed he is, in love of wealth and preference for this world and seeking it, strong and capable, while in love of the worship of Allah and thanking Him for His blessings, he is weak." One says: "He is shadid for this matter and strong for it," when he is capable of it and able to manage it.

Third: he intended: "And indeed he is, in love of good things, not pleasant and expansive, but rather intense and constricted."

Fourth: al-Farra' said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And indeed he is, in love of good, intensely loving," meaning that he loves wealth and loves being one who loves it, but He suffices with the first love over the second, as He said: ﴿The wind has driven him on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning, on a day of stormy wind, so He suffices with the first over the second.

Fifth: Qutrub said: meaning, he is intensely loving of good, as when you say: "He is, for Zayd, a striker," meaning, he is the striker of Zayd.

Al-Wahidi said: The root of kanud (ungrateful) is withholding what is right and good, and the kanud is one who withholds what is owed. And a kanud land is one that produces nothing. Then the exegetes have various expressions. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah said: the kanud is the kafur (ungrateful disbeliever). They said: from it the famous man was named Kindah, because he disowned (kanada) his father and separated from him. And from al-Kalbi: the kanud, in the language of Kindah, is the disobedient one; in the language of Banu Malik, the stingy one; and in the language of Mudar and Rabi'ah, the ungrateful one. Abu Umamah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "the kanud is the ungrateful one who withholds his gift, eats alone, and beats his servant." Al-Hasan said: "al-kanud" is one who complains to his Lord, counting trials and calamities, and forgets blessings and comforts. This is like His saying: ﴿But as for man, when his Lord tries him and honours him and bestows favour upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tries him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ [al-Fajr: 16]. Know that the meaning of kanud does not go beyond being disbelief or wickedness, and in any case it cannot be applied to all people, so it must be restricted to a particular disbeliever. Or, if we apply it to all, the meaning is that human nature inclines him to this, except when Allah protects him from it by His kindness and grace. The first view is that of the majority. They said: because Ibn Abbas said that it was revealed concerning Qurt ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Nawfal al-Qurashi. Also, His saying: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾ befits only the disbeliever, since it is like an indication that he denies that matter.

The second: among the matters over which Allah swore is His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾, and concerning it there are two views:

One: that man, to that (i.e., to his ingratitude), is a witness, testifying against himself to it, either because it is a clear matter that he cannot deny, or because he will testify against himself to it in the Hereafter and acknowledge his sins.

The second view: the intended meaning is "And indeed Allah is, to that, a witness." They said: this is preferable, because the pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned item, and the nearest here is the word "Lord" (Rabb), exalted is He. This would be like a warning and a deterrent to him from disobedience, in that He records his deeds against him. As for those who support the first view, they said: since His following saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾ has its pronoun referring to man, it is necessary that the pronoun in the verse before it also refer to man, so that the arrangement is better.

The third matter over which Allah swore is His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾. Khayr (good) here means wealth, from His saying: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth (khayran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180] and His saying: ﴿And when evil (sharr) touches him, he is despairing﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 21]. This is because people count wealth among themselves as good, just as He, exalted is He, called what the fighter receives of wounds and the harm of war "evil (su')" in His saying: ﴿no harm (su') touched them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 174]. Al-shadid means the stingy, withholding one; it is said: "so-and-so is shadid and mutashaddid." Tarafah said:

I see death seizing the noble and choosing the treasured wealth of the wicked, miserly one.

Then in the interpretation there are several aspects:

One: that because of love of wealth, he is indeed stingy and withholding.

Second: that the intended meaning of shadid is strong, and the meaning is: "And indeed he is, in love of wealth and preference for this world and seeking it, strong and capable, while in love of the worship of Allah and thanking Him for His blessings, he is weak." One says: "He is shadid for this matter and strong for it," when he is capable of it and able to manage it.

Third: he intended: "And indeed he is, in love of good things, not pleasant and expansive, but rather intense and constricted."

Fourth: al-Farra' said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And indeed he is, in love of good, intensely loving," meaning that he loves wealth and loves being one who loves it, but He suffices with the first love over the second, as He said: ﴿The wind has driven him on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], meaning, on a day of stormy wind, so He suffices with the first over the second.

Fifth: Qutrub said: meaning, he is intensely loving of good, as when you say: "He is, for Zayd, a striker," meaning, he is the striker of Zayd.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had enumerated the ugly deeds of the man, He warned him, saying: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: the discussion of "buʿthira" has already passed in His saying: ﴿And when the graves are scattered forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 4]. We mentioned there that the meaning of ﴿buthirat﴾ is "was raised up, stirred up, and brought out." It is also read as "buḥthira."

The second issue: One may ask why He said ﴿what is in the graves﴾ and did not say "who is in the graves." Then, since He said "what," why did He say ﴿Indeed, their Lord, concerning them﴾ and not "Indeed, their Lord, concerning them, on that Day, is All-Knowing"?

The answer to the first question: what is in the earth of those who are not accountable (mukallafun) is more numerous, so He expressed the statement in the more common manner. Or it may be said that when they are raised they are not living rational beings, but after the resurrection they become so. Therefore the first pronoun was that of non-rational beings and the second pronoun was that of rational beings.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, what is in the breasts is distinguished. Al-Layth said: "al-ḥāṣil" from anything is what remains and is established after everything else has gone away, and "al-taḥṣīl" is the distinguishing of what is obtained, and the noun is "al-ḥaṣīla." Labid said:

"And every person, one day, will know his striving
when the ḥaṣāʾil are obtained before God."

In the exegesis there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning of ﴿ḥuṣṣila﴾ is "gathered in the scrolls," that is, they are made manifest as something collected and gathered.

The second: there must be a distinction between the obligatory (wājib), the recommended (mandūb), the permissible (mubāḥ), the disliked (makrūh), and the forbidden (maḥẓūr), for each of them is distinct. From this the sieve was called "al-muḥaṣṣil."

The third: often a person's inner state is contrary to his outward state. But on the Day of Resurrection, secrets will be uncovered and veils will be torn away, and what is in the inner selves will appear, as He said: ﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. Know that the share of admonition from this is that it is said: you prepare for what has no benefit for you. You build the grave, you buy the coffin, you tailor the shroud, and the old woman spins the shroud. It is said: all of this is for the worms, so where is the share for the Most Merciful? Rather, when a woman is pregnant, she prepares garments for the infant. If you say to her, "There is no child for you, so what is this preparation?" she says, "Will what is in my belly not be scattered forth?" Then the Lord says to you, "Will what is in the belly of the earth not be scattered forth? So where is the preparation?"

And it is read as "waḥaṣala" with a fatḥa and without shaddah, meaning "appeared."

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, their Lord is, concerning them, that Day, certainly All-Aware.﴾ Know that there are questions concerning this:

The first: It gives the impression that His knowledge of them on that day came about through experience (ikhtibar, "testing"), and that this requires prior ignorance, which is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. The answer is in two respects:

The first of them: It is as if He, exalted is He, says: whoever was not knowing, becomes knowing through testing; so how could One who has always been knowing not be aware of your conditions!

The second of them: The benefit of specifying that time in His saying ﴿that Day﴾, despite His being knowing eternally, is that it is the time of recompense and of establishing who holds the dominion. It is as if He says: there is no judge whose ruling prevails, and no knower whose verdict is valid on that day, except Him. Many a scholar does not know the answer at the time of the event and then recalls it afterward; so it is as if He, exalted is He, says: I am not like that.

The second question: Why did He single out the deeds of the hearts by mention in His saying ﴿and what is in the breasts is brought out﴾ and omit mention of the deeds of the limbs? The answer: Because the deeds of the limbs follow the deeds of the heart. For were it not for the impulses and intentions in the hearts, the actions of the limbs would not occur. For this reason He, exalted is He, made the heart the root in censure, saying ﴿his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], and the root in praise, saying ﴿their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

The third question: Why did He say ﴿what is in the breasts﴾ and not say "what is in the hearts"? The answer: Because the heart is the mount of the spirit (ruh), and by nature it loves knowing Allah and serving Him. The one who contends in this domain is only the soul (nafs), and its seat is what is near the chest (sadr). For this reason He said ﴿who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 5], and He said ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam...﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], making the breast the place of Islam.

The fourth question: The pronoun in His saying ﴿Indeed, their Lord is, concerning them﴾ refers to al-insan (man), which is singular. The answer: al-insan is in the sense of the plural, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2], then He said ﴿except those who believed﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]; and were it not that it is for the plural, this would not be correct. Know that two more matters remain from the discussions of this verse:

The first matter: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is knowing of the particulars that occur in time, because He explicitly stated His knowledge of the manner of their conditions on that day; so whoever denies this is a disbeliever.

The second matter: It is reported that al-Hajjaj slipped in speech and said "inna bi-l-nasb" (with the accusative), so he dropped the lam from His saying ﴿la-khabir﴾ so that the sentence would not be ungrammatical. This is mentioned in describing his eloquence. Some shaykhs held that this is disbelief, because it is an intention to alter the revealed text. It is reported from Abu al-Samaw'al that he recited in this manner. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
